title: Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party
summary: For seventy-one years one party, under three names, won every presidential election in Mexico. Twelve scenes on how the PRI was built out of a revolution, how it held power, and how it lost it.

scenes.title: Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party
scenes.narration: From 1929 to 2000 one party governed Mexico without a break, winning every presidential election under three successive names. The Institutional Revolutionary Party, the PRI, claimed the legacy of the Mexican Revolution, built a political machine that reached into every union and village, and moved from land reform to free trade while keeping power. This film follows how it was built, how it ruled, how it lost, and what has become of it.

scenes.title: The Revolution, 1910–1920
scenes.narration: In 1910 Francisco Madero called for revolt against Porfirio Díaz, who had ruled Mexico for more than thirty years. A decade of civil war followed, in which peasant armies under Emiliano Zapata in the south and Francisco Villa in the north fought first alongside and then against the constitutionalist generals of Coahuila and Sonora. The constitution of 1917 promised land reform, workers' rights and national ownership of the subsoil, and the Sonoran generals who came out on top, Álvaro Obregón and Plutarco Elías Calles, ruled through the 1920s.

scenes.title: From strongmen to a party, 1928–1929
scenes.narration: In July 1928 Obregón, just re-elected president, was assassinated by a Catholic militant during the Cristero rebellion against the government's anti-clerical laws. In his last address to Congress that September, Calles called on Mexico to pass from rule by strongmen to a nation of institutions and laws. In March 1929 he founded the National Revolutionary Party to unite the revolution's regional bosses and generals, and through the years known as the Maximato he remained the power behind three short-lived presidents.

scenes.title: Cárdenas remakes the party, 1934–1940
scenes.narration: Lázaro Cárdenas, president from 1934, broke with Calles and sent him into exile in 1936. He distributed about 18 million hectares of land to peasant communities, backed a new national labour confederation, and on 18 March 1938 expropriated the foreign oil companies, a day still celebrated in Mexico. That month he rebuilt the party as the Party of the Mexican Revolution, organised in sectors for peasants, workers, the army and the middle classes, a corporatist structure that tied millions of Mexicans to it.

scenes.title: The PRI system, 1946–1970
scenes.narration: Renamed the Institutional Revolutionary Party in January 1946, with a civilian, Miguel Alemán, as its presidential candidate, the party presided over growth of around six per cent a year until about 1970, the so-called Mexican miracle. Presidents served a single six-year term, as the constitution required, and by an unwritten rule each chose his own successor, the dedazo or tap of the finger, whom voters then elected by overwhelming margins. Beatriz Magaloni argues that the PRI survived less by fraud than by patronage, divided opponents and voters' fear of what turning against it might cost them.

scenes.title: Tlatelolco, 1968
scenes.narration: The system also rested on repression. On 2 October 1968, ten days before the Olympic Games opened in Mexico City, soldiers and security agents opened fire on a student rally in the Plaza of the Three Cultures at Tlatelolco. The government's spokesman spoke of 20 dead; a search of the official archives led by Kate Doyle in 2006 confirmed 44, while the figure most often repeated, about 300, has never been documented. In the dirty war that followed against left-wing guerrillas and dissidents, a special prosecutor's report of 2006 named the victims of 645 disappearances.

scenes.title: Crisis, and the election of 1988
scenes.narration: The debt crisis of 1982 ended an oil-fuelled boom, and the government's slow response to the Mexico City earthquake of 1985 fed a new civic opposition. In 1987 Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, the former president's son, left the PRI to run for president on the left, and on election night in July 1988 the count stopped when the computer system was said to have crashed. Carlos Salinas was declared the winner with just over half the vote, a result his opponents never accepted, and Congress later had the ballots burned.

scenes.title: Free trade and the perfect dictatorship
scenes.narration: Salinas privatised hundreds of state companies and the banks, opened the economy and negotiated the North American Free Trade Agreement with the United States and Canada. In August 1990 the Peruvian novelist Mario Vargas Llosa, speaking on Mexican television, called Mexico the perfect dictatorship, a camouflaged one in which not a man but a party stayed in power. His host, the poet Octavio Paz, objected that Mexico had known the hegemony of one party but not a dictatorship, and none of the military dictatorships seen elsewhere in Latin America.

visual.text: Mexico is the perfect dictatorship. The perfect dictatorship is not communism. It is not the USSR. It is not Fidel Castro. The perfect dictatorship is Mexico.

scenes.title: 1994: rebellion, murder and a crash
scenes.narration: On 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA came into force, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation rose in Chiapas in the name of the indigenous poor. In March the PRI's presidential candidate, Luis Donaldo Colosio, was shot dead at a rally in Tijuana, and in September the party's secretary-general was murdered too. Ernesto Zedillo won the presidency in August, but within weeks of his taking office a run on the peso plunged Mexico into its worst recession in decades.

scenes.title: Defeat, 2000
scenes.narration: Zedillo allowed the electoral institute full independence in 1996, and in 1997 the PRI lost its majority in the Chamber of Deputies for the first time. On 2 July 2000 Vicente Fox of the conservative National Action Party won the presidency, and Zedillo conceded on television that night, ending seventy-one years of PRI rule peacefully. Kenneth Greene argues that the PRI lost once it could no longer draw on public resources to outspend its opponents and keep them on the margins.

visual.note: Official results as shares of valid votes (spoiled ballots left out), including allied parties' votes for the same candidate: Nohlen to 2000, then the official counts. The PRI's predecessor stood in 1934; it lost the presidency in 2000, 2006 and 2018.

scenes.title: Return and collapse, 2012–2024
scenes.narration: The PRI kept its strength in the states, and in 2012 Enrique Peña Nieto won back the presidency, carried, as Joy Langston explains, by the party's governors and their machines. His Pact for Mexico with the main opposition parties brought reforms of education and telecommunications, and in 2013 the oil industry was opened to private investment, but the disappearance of 43 students from the Ayotzinapa teachers' college in 2014 and a run of corruption scandals cost the party dearly. In 2018 Andrés Manuel López Obrador's new party, Morena, won a landslide and the PRI's candidate came third. In 2024, even in alliance with its old rival the National Action Party, the PRI won only 35 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies.

scenes.title: The PRI's legacy
scenes.narration: Mexico's democracy grew out of the PRI's long decline, as independent electoral authorities, competitive state elections and a freer press were won step by step. Historians still argue over the party's record, between the stability, mass schooling and land reform it oversaw and the corruption, fraud and violence that sustained it. Political scientists study it as the model of a dominant party that ruled through elections, and of how such a party can lose them.
